qs.q: Which restriction applies to the enjoyment of freedom of speech in democratic states?
o: Prohibition against criticizing statutory tax rates
Requirement to obtain police approval before speaking
Mandatory endorsement of ruling party candidates
Prohibition against defamation, sedition, and incitement to violence
qs.e: Free speech is subject to lawful limitations against defamation, libel, sedition, and hate speech.

qs.q: The legal concept of 'Eminent Domain' empowers the state to compulsory acquire private property for public use provided
o: the owner belongs to the ruling political party
the property is located inside the national capital
no opposition party members reside nearby
prompt and fair compensation is paid to the owner
qs.e: Eminent domain allows compulsory acquisition for public interest subject to constitutional compensation requirements.

qs.q: Judicial immunity protects judges from personal civil lawsuits arising from decisions made in their
qs.e: Judicial immunity protects judges from personal liability for judicial acts performed in good faith.

qs.q: The Customary Court of Appeal in Nigeria exercises appellate jurisdiction over civil proceedings involving questions of
qs.e: Customary Courts of Appeal hear cases arising from traditional customary personal and land law.

qs.q: The Sharia Court of Appeal exercises specialized appellate jurisdiction over civil cases concerning
qs.e: Sharia Courts of Appeal deal exclusively with matters of Islamic personal and family law.

qs.q: The legal doctrine of 'Coram Non Judice' applies when a court proceedings are conducted without proper
o: written records taken down in shorthand
jurisdiction, rendering the entire judgment a nullity
qs.e: Coram non judice ('not before a judge') invalidates proceedings conducted by a court lacking legal jurisdiction.

qs.q: In constitutional interpretation, the 'Living Tree Doctrine' posits that the constitution should be interpreted as an
o: unchangeable set of medieval religious commands
literal word-for-word strict text frozen in time
informal collection of party political guidelines
organic document that evolves to address contemporary societal realities
qs.e: Living tree doctrine views constitutional text as dynamic and adaptable to changing modern conditions.

qs.q: The 'Original Intent' doctrine of constitutional interpretation asserts that judges must interpret provisions strictly according to the
o: latest public opinion polls published in newspapers
economic preferences of major corporate sponsors
foreign policy directives of allied states
intentions of the original framers at the time of drafting
qs.e: Original intent insists on interpreting constitutional language based on historical meaning understood by framers.

qs.q: The prerogative writ of 'Writ of Quo Warranto' literally translates from Latin as
qs.e: Quo warranto means 'by what warrant/authority', demanding proof of entitlement to hold public office.

qs.q: The 'Purposive Approach' to statutory interpretation requires judges to interpret legislation in a manner that best promotes the
o: literal dictionary meaning of every individual word regardless of absurdity
personal political preferences of the presiding judge
underlying purpose and legislative intent of the statute
qs.e: Purposive interpretation looks beyond literal wording to fulfill the genuine statutory purpose intended by parliament.

qs.q: A political party is defined in government as an organized group of citizens seeking to win control of
qs.e: Political parties organize citizens with shared beliefs to contest elections and form government.

qs.q: A pressure group differs from a political party primarily because a pressure group does not seek to
o: contest elections or directly form government
educate the general public on social issues
qs.e: Pressure groups aim to influence policy decisions without directly contesting elections to capture state office.

qs.q: Which party system allows only one political party to operate legally within the state?
qs.e: One-party systems legally ban opposition political parties, concentrating political power in a single party.

qs.q: A multi-party system is a political framework where three or more political parties have a realistic chance of
o: winning legislative seats and forming government
qs.e: Multi-party systems permit multiple political parties to compete freely for legislative and executive power.

qs.q: Public opinion refers to the collective views, attitudes, and beliefs held by citizens on matters of
qs.e: Public opinion reflects the aggregate views of citizens regarding political issues, state policies, and leaders.

qs.q: Pressure groups whose primary goal is to protect the economic or professional interests of their members are called
qs.e: Sectional pressure groups (e.g. trade unions, professional associations) represent specific economic or occupational interests.

qs.q: Political party manifestos serve as official public documents outlining party
qs.e: A party manifesto presents the party's ideological stance, policy objectives, and promises to voters.

qs.q: An essential function of political parties in a representative democracy is political recruitment, which involves
o: selecting and training candidates for public elective office
appointing senior officers into the armed forces
recruiting administrative staff for foreign embassies
managing private sector commercial bank branches
qs.e: Political parties identify, groom, and nominate suitable candidates to run for political positions.

qs.q: Unlike sectional interest groups, cause or promotional pressure groups direct their advocacy toward
o: causes that benefit society generally rather than specific members
exclusive wage increases for trade union executives
monopolistic trade privileges for corporate cartels
qs.e: Cause groups (e.g. human rights or environmental groups) advocate broader social issues benefiting the public.

qs.q: Mass parties are political parties that seek to enlist widespread membership across all social classes and rely on
o: exclusive financial sponsorship by wealthy industrial barons
compulsory deductions from civil service salaries
qs.e: Mass parties feature expansive membership bases, decentralized branch networks, and popular financial support.

qs.q: Elitist or cadre parties differ from mass parties because cadre parties depend on a small, highly select group of
qs.e: Cadre parties restrict formal membership to influential figures, relying on elite prestige rather than mass numbers.

qs.q: Which strategy is commonly employed by pressure groups to directly influence legislative lawmakers?
o: Lobbying parliamentary committees and presenting technical briefs
Organizing military coups against elected governments
qs.e: Lobbying provides technical expertise and arguments to persuade lawmakers during legislative deliberations.

qs.q: Anomic pressure groups are short-lived, unorganized groups that emerge spontaneously in response to a specific crisis, often resorting to
o: filing civil suits in supreme courts
qs.e: Anomic groups form spontaneously during heightened tension, expressing grievances through sudden protests.

qs.q: Institutional pressure groups exist within formal state structures or organizations, such as the
qs.e: Institutional groups operate inside established bodies (like the army or civil service) to protect institutional interests.

qs.q: A major factor shaping public opinion in modern democratic societies is the mass media, including
o: newspapers, radio, television, and digital platforms
qs.e: Mass media channels report news, analyze policy, and provide platforms that inform public opinion.

qs.q: In a two-party system, political stability is generally maintained because two dominant parties alternate in controlling the
qs.e: Two-party systems concentrate voting between two major parties, usually producing clear government majorities.

qs.q: Which condition can undermine the effectiveness of pressure group activities in a state?
o: High literacy rates among general citizens
Authoritarian government suppression of civil liberties and public dissent
Existence of private media broadcasting stations
qs.e: Repressive authoritarian regimes suppress free assembly and advocacy, severely curtailing pressure group impact.

qs.q: Propaganda is a technique used by political parties and governments to influence public opinion through
qs.e: Propaganda uses persuasive, often selective messaging to shape public perception and political support.

qs.q: Political parties facilitate aggregate demand in political systems by combining diverse societal interests into
qs.e: Interest aggregation synthesizes varied demands into unified national policy proposals.

qs.q: The concept of 'Iron Law of Oligarchy' formulated by Robert Michels posits that all complex organizations, including political parties, eventually become dominated by a
o: broad democratic vote of general members
qs.e: Michels argued that organizational complexity inevitably concentrates practical decision-making in leadership elites.

qs.q: Which characteristic distinguishes institutionalized pressure groups from anomic pressure groups?
o: Permanent organizational structure and continuous formal operation
Total reliance on violent street demonstrations
Lack of designated leaders or rules
qs.e: Institutionalized pressure groups possess formal leadership, offices, financial budgets, and long-term continuity.

qs.q: A dominant-party system is a political framework where multiple parties compete, but one party consistently wins control of
qs.e: In dominant-party systems, opposition parties operate legally but struggle to overcome the ruling party's dominance.

qs.q: How do pressure groups contribute to democratic governance?
o: By replacing elected parliamentary legislators in passing statutes
By providing specialized feedback and acting as a check on government power
qs.e: Pressure groups articulate specific grievances, provide technical data, and hold state officials accountable.

qs.q: Which method used by pressure groups involves withholding labor to compel employers or government to grant demands?
qs.e: Strikes temporarily halt work to exercise economic leverage during collective bargaining or policy disputes.

qs.q: Public opinion polling measures citizen attitudes scientifically by surveying a representative sample of the
qs.e: Scientific polling uses representative sampling techniques to gauge public sentiment on political issues.

qs.q: Party discipline refers to the ability of a political party to compel its elected legislative members to
o: resign from public office immediately after election
vote according to official party policy and leadership directives
appoint family members into civil service
qs.e: Party discipline maintains unity, ensuring lawmakers support party bills and executive measures in parliament.

qs.q: Which factor can cause a political party to experience internal factionalism?
o: Uniform agreement on all policy objectives
Ideological disagreements and intense leadership rivalries
qs.e: Conflicting ideological currents and ambition for party executive positions provoke internal factional splits.

qs.q: The term 'astroturfing' in pressure group politics describes creating the false impression of a widespread
qs.e: Astroturfing uses funded public relations campaigns to fake genuine grassroots citizen activism.

qs.q: Civil society organizations (CSOs) strengthen democracy by fostering civic engagement, advocating human rights, and monitoring
qs.e: CSOs act as vital intermediaries between citizens and state, promoting transparency and human rights.

qs.q: When a pressure group files an 'Amicus Curiae' brief in court, it is acting as a
o: prosecuting police officer demanding summary conviction
defense attorney representing a private criminal accused
friend of the court offering expert legal arguments on public interest issues
qs.e: Amicus curiae ('friend of the court') briefs provide non-party expert analysis to assist courts in public interest cases.

qs.q: Which drawback is associated with multi-party systems operating without a dominant party?
o: Concentration of all legislative power in a single monarch
Frequent coalition government instability and policy deadlock
Absence of voter choice during general elections
qs.e: Multi-party systems without clear majorities can produce fragile coalition cabinets prone to frequent collapse.

qs.q: The primary source of funding for promotional pressure groups advocating environmental protection is usually
o: compulsory tax deductions enforced by central state police
statutory budgetary allocations from national assembly
voluntary donations, grants, and membership dues
direct subsidies from foreign military alliances
qs.e: Promotional groups rely on public donations, philanthropic grants, and member contributions to maintain independence.

qs.q: Political party polarization occurs when political parties move toward extreme ideological positions, reducing
o: voter turnout during general national elections
the number of registered civil service staff
the frequency of supreme court sessions
qs.e: Polarization widens ideological gaps, making inter-party compromise and legislative consensus difficult.

qs.q: Which technique is used by pressure groups to mobilize public sympathy and pressure decision-makers?
o: Mass media publicity campaigns and public rallies
qs.e: Public rallies and media campaigns raise awareness, shaping public sentiment to influence policy-makers.

qs.q: Comparing political parties and pressure groups, political parties have a broader policy focus, whereas pressure groups focus on
qs.e: Parties articulate comprehensive platforms covering all state governance, while pressure groups target specific issues.

qs.q: The concept of 'hyperpluralism' in political science describes a situation where pressure groups become so powerful that
o: political parties are completely abolished by law
the judiciary absorbs all executive powers
government policy becomes paralyzed and unable to act effectively
qs.e: Hyperpluralism asserts that competing interest groups immobilize government, creating policy gridlock.

qs.q: In political party dynamics, 'cartel party' theory suggests that established political parties increasingly rely on state subsidies and resources rather than
qs.e: Cartel parties integrate into the state apparatus, drawing public funding and distancing themselves from grassroots voters.

qs.q: Which risk arises when wealthy interest groups exercise disproportionate influence over campaign financing?
o: Immediate collapse of the civil service administration
Automatic conversion of presidential systems to monarchies
Political inequality and policy distortion benefiting elite interests
Total elimination of national import tariffs
qs.e: Unchecked money in politics allows wealthy donors to capture policy outcomes, marginalizing ordinary citizens.

qs.q: The term 'gatekeeping' by news media in shaping public opinion refers to the power to decide which
o: judges are promoted to the supreme court
civil servants receive annual salary raises
stories and perspectives are presented to the public
qs.e: Media gatekeepers filter information, deciding which political issues receive public attention.

qs.q: Which strategy is employed by insider pressure groups that distinguishes them from outsider groups?
o: Organizing disruptive street blockades and strikes
Maintaining regular, privileged access to government ministers and civil servants
qs.e: Insider groups enjoy formal consultation rights and direct access to policymakers, unlike confrontational outsider groups.

qs.q: Outsider pressure groups lack direct government consultation channels and therefore rely primarily on
o: public demonstrations, media stunts, and popular mobilization
qs.e: Lacking administrative access, outsider groups build popular pressure through protests and public campaigns.

qs.q: A referendum is an electoral instrument of direct democracy where the entire electorate votes directly on a specific
o: list of individual civil service promotion candidates
qs.e: Referendums submit crucial public policy or constitutional questions directly to popular vote.

qs.q: An initiative is a direct democratic process that empowers citizens to propose new legislation or constitutional amendments by collecting a required number of
o: judicial affidavits from high court judges
qs.e: Initiatives allow voters to bypass reluctant legislatures by placing proposed laws directly on ballots via petition.

qs.q: The principle of 'peak associations' in interest group representation refers to umbrella organizations that coordinate multiple
o: trade unions or business associations under a single national body
qs.e: Peak associations (e.g. Nigerian Labour Congress or NACCIMA) aggregate allied interest groups nationally.

qs.q: Which condition is necessary for public opinion to effectively constrain government actions?
o: Mandatory state censorship of private news networks
Free press, open access to information, and protection of speech rights
qs.e: Public opinion restrains leaders only when citizens enjoy free speech, open news media, and competitive elections.

qs.q: The 'corporatist' model of interest representation differs from the 'pluralist' model because corporatism involves formal institutional partnership between
o: competing private firms operating without state contact
unorganized citizen street protesters and municipal police
supreme court judges and foreign diplomatic envoys
government, major trade unions, and business peak associations in policymaking
qs.e: Corporatism integrates state officials and major labor/business peak associations into structured policy negotiation.

qs.q: Giovanni Sartori's typology of party systems categorizes systems based on the number of relevant parties and the degree of
o: physical land mass area of electoral districts
number of staff employed by electoral commissions
total tax revenue generated by state enterprises
qs.e: Sartori evaluated party systems by counting relevant parties and measuring ideological polarization.

qs.q: The 'Free-Rider Problem' in interest group theory, formulated by Mancur Olson, explains why individuals may choose not to join a group when they can enjoy benefits without
qs.e: Olson showed that rational individuals exploit collective goods without contributing, hindering group mobilization.

qs.q: To overcome the Free-Rider Problem, interest groups frequently offer selective incentives, which are benefits provided exclusively to
o: all general voters across the state
supreme court judges and court clerks
qs.e: Selective incentives (e.g. legal aid, specialized insurance, discounts) entice individuals to join interest groups.

qs.q: The concept of 'cleavage theory' in political party formation, advanced by Lipset and Rokkan, posits that national party systems reflect historical social splits such as
o: legislative lower house versus upper house staff
police force versus army officer corps
state judicial judges versus private lawyers
center versus periphery, state versus church, and owner versus worker
qs.e: Lipset and Rokkan demonstrated that modern party systems are rooted in historical societal cleavages.

qs.q: Franchise or suffrage in political science refers to the constitutional right of a citizen to
o: hold executive presidential office without contest
qs.e: Franchise is the legal right of eligible citizens to vote for political representatives or policy measures.

qs.q: Universal adult suffrage grants the right to vote to all adult citizens regardless of
o: gender, property, race, or social status
qs.e: Universal adult suffrage eliminates property, gender, or racial restrictions, extending voting rights to all adult citizens.

qs.q: An electoral system is the legal set of rules that governs how votes are cast in an election and converted into
qs.e: Electoral systems define voting procedures and mathematical methods for allocating political office based on votes.

qs.q: The First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) or simple majority electoral system awards victory to the candidate who secures the
o: highest number of votes among contestants
absolute majority of over fifty percent of all votes cast
unanimous endorsement of all electoral officers
majority of votes in every single constituency
qs.e: Under FPTP, the candidate with more votes than any other single contestant wins, regardless of absolute majority.

qs.q: An independent electoral commission is established in a state to organize, conduct, and supervise free and fair
qs.e: Electoral commissions manage voter registration, candidate nomination, ballot logistics, and election result declaration.

qs.q: Secret ballot voting ensures that electors cast their votes in privacy, protecting them from intimidation and
qs.e: Secret balloting keeps individual voter choices confidential, safeguarding electors against threats or vote-buying pressure.

qs.q: A general election is a nationwide electoral exercise in which voters select representatives for national or regional
qs.e: General elections choose national or state leaders and parliamentarians across all constituencies.

qs.q: Proportional Representation (PR) is an electoral system designed to allocate legislative seats to political parties based on the
o: percentage of total votes received by each party
geographical size of state territory controlled
number of military officers sponsoring the party
total property taxes paid by party leaders
qs.e: PR systems ensure party seat shares in parliament mirror their overall share of the popular vote.

qs.q: An absolute majority electoral system requires a winning candidate to secure more than
o: fifty percent of the total votes cast
qs.e: Absolute majority systems demand fifty percent plus one vote (50%+1) to declare a candidate elected.

qs.q: A run-off or second-ballot election is conducted when no candidate secures the required absolute majority in the
qs.e: If no candidate achieves an absolute majority initially, a second election pits the top two vote-getters against each other.

qs.q: Which type of franchise restricted voting rights historically to citizens possessing specified land or wealth?
qs.e: Property qualification historically limited suffrage to wealthy landowners or taxpayers.

qs.q: By-elections are special elections conducted to fill a legislative vacancy caused by the death, resignation, or disqualification of an
qs.e: By-elections choose replacement lawmakers when legislative seats become vacant between general elections.

qs.q: Voter registration is the administrative process of compiling an official list of eligible citizens entitled to
qs.e: Compiling a voter register prevents illegal voting and ensures only eligible citizens cast ballots.

qs.q: Which factor can cause voter apathy and low turnout during elections?
o: Widespread public distrust in electoral integrity and rampant political corruption
qs.e: Citizens abstain from voting when they believe elections are rigged or leaders are unaccountable.

qs.q: Electoral malpractice refers to illegal or fraudulent activities that corrupt the integrity of the electoral process, such as
o: ballot box stuffing, vote-buying, and falsification of results
qs.e: Malpractice undermines democratic legitimacy through fraudulent voting, intimidation, or result manipulation.

qs.q: Constituency delineation involves dividing the territory of a state into distinct geographical units for the purpose of
qs.e: Delineation establishes electoral boundaries to ensure equitable representation across population centers.

qs.q: Primary elections are internal party processes held to select party candidates who will contest in
qs.e: Parties conduct primary elections or caucuses to choose official nominees for upcoming public elections.

qs.q: Which voting procedure requires electors to physically line up behind candidates or their symbols?
qs.e: Open balloting makes individual voter choices visible, with electors queuing behind preferred candidates.

qs.q: Proxy voting allows an eligible voter who is unable to attend polling in person to authorize a designated representative to
o: cast a vote on their behalf
qs.e: Proxy voting permits designated proxies to cast ballots for electors unable to attend due to illness or distance.

qs.q: The Single Transferable Vote (STV) system is a proportional representation method that uses multi-member constituencies and allows voters to
o: vote for an entire party list without choosing candidates
rank candidates in order of preference
cast a single unalterable vote for a monarch
qs.e: STV enables voters to rank candidates numerically, transferring surplus votes above winning quotas to lower preferences.

qs.q: The Party List PR system allocates legislative seats to political parties based on predefined ordered lists of candidates prepared by
qs.e: In Party List PR, parties present candidate lists and win seats proportional to their national vote percentage.

qs.q: Which condition is vital for an electoral commission to maintain public confidence?
o: Total financial dependency on ruling party donations
Operational, financial, and political independence from executive control
Secret counting of ballot papers without observers
qs.e: Independent funding and autonomous administration insulate electoral commissions from political bias.

qs.q: Malapportionment occurs when electoral constituencies are created with vastly unequal population sizes, violating the principle of
qs.e: Malapportionment creates unequal district sizes, giving voters in smaller districts disproportionate influence.

qs.q: Which device allows citizens residing abroad to participate in national elections of their home state?
qs.e: Diaspora voting extends electoral participation to citizens living overseas through embassies or postal ballots.

qs.q: The term 'Electoral Threshold' in proportional representation systems refers to the minimum percentage of national votes a party must win to
qs.e: Electoral thresholds prevent excessive legislative fragmentation by requiring parties to secure a minimum vote share (e.g. 5%).

qs.q: Which advantage is associated with First-Past-The-Post electoral systems?
o: It guarantees exact proportional seat distribution for minority parties
It usually produces clear single-party legislative majorities and stable governments
It eliminates the need for constituency boundaries
qs.e: FPTP tends to produce decisive single-party majorities, avoiding complex coalition bargaining.

qs.q: A key criticism of First-Past-The-Post systems is that they often produce 'wasted votes' and result in
o: excessive representation for minor fringe parties
disproportionate representation where winning parties gain seat shares far exceeding vote shares
qs.e: FPTP creates disproportional results, penalizing small third parties whose votes do not yield constituency victories.

qs.q: Alternative Vote (AV) or preferential voting requires voters in single-member districts to rank candidates, reallocating lowest vote-getters' preferences until a candidate achieves an
qs.e: AV reallocates secondary preferences of eliminated candidates until one contestant achieves an absolute majority.

qs.q: Which institution is responsible for resolving legal disputes and petitions arising from election results in Nigeria?
qs.e: Election petition tribunals adjudicate legal challenges regarding election validity, candidate qualifications, and result declarations.

qs.q: The 'Option A-4' voting system used historically in Nigeria involved open voting starting from the ward level up to the
qs.e: Option A-4 instituted staged open-ballot selection from ward to national level to determine presidential nominees.

qs.q: Compulsory voting is a legal requirement in some democracies where citizens are required by law to
o: register and cast a vote on election day or face statutory fines
serve as polling station presiding officers
qs.e: Compulsory voting mandates voter participation, imposing minor fines or administrative penalties on non-voters.

qs.q: Which factor promotes electoral integrity during ballot counting?
o: Excluding all political party agents from counting rooms
Conducting result collation in secret military locations
Presence of accredited party agents, media journalists, and independent observers at collation centers
Destroying ballot papers immediately after voting
qs.e: Open counting in the presence of party agents and observers deters fraud and ensures result transparency.

qs.q: An electoral register audit is conducted prior to elections to detect and remove
o: voters who belong to opposition political parties
citizens who do not own real estate property
underage voters, deceased persons, and duplicate registrations
civil servants working in executive ministries
qs.e: Voter register audits clean data, eliminating illegitimate entries to ensure a credible voter roll.

qs.q: Snap elections are general elections called earlier than the scheduled official term end, usually initiated by the
o: Prime Minister or executive in a parliamentary system
qs.e: Parliamentary executives call snap elections to capitalize on favorable public opinion or resolve parliamentary deadlocks.

qs.q: Maurice Duverger's Law in political science states that First-Past-The-Post electoral systems tend to favor a
qs.e: Duverger's Law demonstrates that FPTP mechanically and strategically disadvantages third parties, favoring two-party systems.

qs.q: Conversely, Duverger's hypothesis suggests that Proportional Representation electoral systems tend to foster a
qs.e: Proportional representation allows smaller parties to gain legislative representation, encouraging multi-party competition.

qs.q: The 'Droop Quota' is a mathematical formula used in Single Transferable Vote systems to calculate the minimum number of votes required for a candidate to win a
qs.e: The Droop Quota formula (Votes / (Seats + 1)) + 1 sets the exact vote threshold needed to secure a seat in STV.

qs.q: Which phenomenon occurs when voters abandon their preferred third-party candidate to vote for a less-preferred major party candidate to prevent a worse outcome?
qs.e: Tactical voting occurs when electors cast votes strategically for viable major candidates rather than preferred minor candidates.

qs.q: A 'spoasted' or invalid ballot paper is a ballot that cannot be counted because it is
o: cast by a female adult citizen
marked with blue ink instead of black ink
submitted by a civil service staff member
unclear, improperly marked, or contains identifying marks violating secret balloting
qs.e: Invalid ballots are rejected during counting due to improper marking, multiple votes, or breach of secrecy.

qs.q: Which requirement is designed to ensure that a winning presidential candidate possesses broad national support across a federal state?
o: Winning unanimous support in the national capital territory only
Obtaining endorsement from the military high command
Securing highest votes in the wealthiest state only
Securing both an absolute majority of total votes and a minimum percentage of votes across a specified fraction of states
qs.e: Federal presidential requirements (e.g. 25% of votes in two-thirds of states) ensure broad geopolitical appeal.

qs.q: Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and biometric voter verification are implemented to reduce human error and eliminate
o: the need for political party manifestos
qs.e: Biometric verification confirms voter identity, preventing multiple voting and impersonation at polling stations.

qs.q: An electoral code of conduct is an agreement signed by political parties to promote peaceful campaigning and prohibit
o: hate speech, voter intimidation, and political violence
qs.e: Electoral codes establish behavioral norms for parties, curbing inflammatory rhetoric and election violence.

qs.q: Which drawback is associated with Proportional Representation systems?
o: They systematically underrepresent minority political groups
They produce massive single-party legislative landslides routinely
They eliminate opposition parties from parliament
They can grant excessive leverage to small extremist fringe parties in coalition bargaining
qs.e: PR systems can allow small key parties to hold disproportionate leverage when forming coalition governments.

qs.q: The 'Mixed-Member Proportional' (MMP) electoral system combines elements of First-Past-The-Post single-member districts with
qs.e: MMP combines constituency voting via FPTP with compensatory party list seats to achieve overall proportionality.

qs.q: Which factor poses the greatest threat to free and fair elections in developing democracies?
o: High voter turnout across rural farming communities
Active participation of international observer missions
Transparent live broadcasting of collation results
Pervasive vote-buying, security agency bias, and executive interference with electoral bodies
qs.e: Monetary corruption, compromised electoral independence, and partisan security operations severely corrupt election integrity.

qs.q: The 'Sainte-Laguë' and 'D'Hondt' methods are mathematical highest-averages formulas used in Proportional Representation to calculate
o: campaign finance expenditure limits for candidates
salary scales for electoral polling clerks
qs.e: D'Hondt and Sainte-Laguë are mathematical algorithms used to allocate parliamentary seats based on vote tallies in PR.

qs.q: In electoral analysis, the 'Cube Law' posits that in First-Past-The-Post two-party systems, the ratio of seats won by two major parties is proportional to the
o: square root of total registered voters
arithmetic sum of state electoral districts
logarithm of national GDP growth rate
cube of the ratio of votes won by each party
qs.e: The Cube Law demonstrates mathematically how FPTP amplifies small vote leads into large legislative seat majorities.

qs.q: The concept of 'Electoral Volatility' measures the net change in voter support across political parties between
o: different primary nomination rounds within one party
qs.e: Electoral volatility calculates shift in voter allegiance from one election to the next, indicating party system stability.

qs.q: Rae's Index of Fractionalization measures the degree of political fragmentation in a party system based on the number of parties and their
o: number of staff employed in regional offices
average age of party executive members
relative share of votes or seats
qs.e: Rae's Index quantifies party system fragmentation by assessing vote and seat distribution across competing parties.

qs.q: The 'Gallagher Index' is a recognized statistical formula used by political scientists to measure the degree of electoral disproportionality between
o: registered voters and actual votes cast
campaign funds raised and spent by candidates
male and female candidates contesting elections
votes received and seats allocated to political parties
qs.e: The Gallagher Index measures disproportionality between popular vote percentages and resulting legislative seat shares.

qs.q: The Civil Service is the permanent administrative body of career public officials employed to implement government
qs.e: The civil service forms the permanent administrative engine of executive government departments.

qs.q: Which characteristics traditionally define the Civil Service in a democratic state?
o: Military discipline, secrecy, and commercial profit
Electoral competition, political campaign advocacy, and wealth
qs.e: Civil service principles center on tenure permanence, political neutrality, and administrative anonymity.

qs.q: Administrative anonymity means that civil servants carry out official duties behind the public figure of the
o: political minister, who takes public praise or blame
qs.e: Anonymity shields civil servants from public political criticism, placing official responsibility on elected ministers.

qs.q: Civil service neutrality requires administrative staff to serve the elected government of the day with total loyalty regardless of their own
qs.e: Neutrality ensures civil servants render impartial professional service to whichever political party holds power.

qs.q: Within a state ministry in Nigeria, the administrative civil service leadership is provided by the
qs.e: The Permanent Secretary is the senior career civil servant directing ministry operations and financial management.

qs.q: The Civil Service Commission is an independent statutory body established to handle recruitment, promotion, and
qs.e: Civil Service Commissions oversee merit-based recruitment, career advancement, and disciplinary control of public servants.

qs.q: Bureaucracy is an administrative organizational structure characterized by hierarchical authority, standardized rules, and specialized
qs.e: Bureaucracy organizes complex public administration through formal hierarchies, explicit rules, and functional specialization.

qs.q: Permanence of tenure in the civil service implies that civil servants retain their employment despite changes in the
qs.e: Permanence guarantees career continuity across changing political administrations, preserving institutional memory.

qs.q: The Merit System in civil service recruitment ensures that candidates are appointed and promoted based on
o: educational qualifications, competence, and performance examination
political party patronage and campaign loyalty
qs.e: Merit-based administration evaluates applicants on tested skill and qualifications rather than political favoritism.

qs.q: Political patronage or the 'Spoils System' refers to the practice of appointing loyal party supporters to public administrative positions regardless of
qs.e: The spoils system rewards political allies with public offices, often compromising administrative efficiency.

qs.q: Red tape in bureaucratic administration refers to excessive adherence to formal rules and procedures, resulting in
qs.e: Red tape describes rigid procedural formalities that slow down administrative processes and frustrate citizens.

qs.q: Which class in the civil service hierarchy consists of top managerial career officials responsible for policy advice and departmental management?
qs.e: The Administrative Class occupies the top tier, assisting ministers with policy formulation and departmental leadership.

qs.q: The Executive Class in the civil service is primarily responsible for day-to-day enforcement and implementation of established
qs.e: The Executive Class handles routine administrative execution, managing accounts, records, and operational tasks.

qs.q: Which class in the civil service performs routine tasks such as filing, typing, and record-keeping?
qs.e: The Clerical Class provides essential office support, handling correspondence, filing, and routine record management.

qs.q: The General Orders or Public Service Rules contain statutory regulations governing the conduct, rights, and duties of
qs.e: Public Service Rules codify employment conditions, code of conduct, disciplinary steps, and privileges for civil servants.

qs.q: Whistleblowing mechanisms in public administration protect civil servants who report internal acts of
o: corruption, fraud, and illegal administrative practices

Total absence of agricultural farming in the North

qs.q: The 'Sarkin Fada' in the Hausa-Fulani Emirate administration held the official title of
o: Palace Administrative Head and Chief of Staff
qs.e: Sarkin Fada managed royal palace administration, domestic staff, and access to the Emir.

qs.q: The 'Sarkin Ruwa' in the Hausa-Fulani administrative system was responsible for supervising
qs.e: Sarkin Ruwa managed river resources, fishing rights, and water transport in the emirate.

qs.q: In the pre-colonial Benin Kingdom, the 'Oliha' held the chief position as the leader of the
qs.e: Chief Oliha led the Uzama council, performing the crowning rites for new Obas.

qs.q: The 'Iwebo', 'Iweguae', and 'Ibiwe' represented the three major palace administrative societies in the pre-colonial
qs.e: These three palace guilds managed royal wardrobe, domestic affairs, and royal harem in Benin.

qs.q: The Etsu was the supreme traditional monarch in the pre-colonial political system of the
qs.e: The Etsu Nupe headed the centralized Nupe Kingdom centered at Bida.

qs.q: The Attah was the traditional supreme ruler of the pre-colonial
qs.e: The Attah of Igala ruled the centralized Igala Kingdom centered at Idah.

qs.q: In the pre-colonial Efik political system of Old Calabar, civil governance and trade regulation were heavily enforced by the
qs.e: Ekpe society acted as the primary administrative, judicial, and law-enforcement authority in Efik city-states.

qs.q: Which feature distinguished pre-colonial African segmentary societies from centralized states?
o: Complete lack of laws, customs, or social order
Total reliance on foreign European mercenaries for defense
Absolute rule by a single military dictator
Absence of a single permanent monarch and diffusion of power among lineage elders and assemblies
qs.e: Segmentary societies maintained order through lineage councils, age grades, and title societies rather than a single king.

qs.q: The 'Etsu Bida' and 'Etsu Agaie' were prominent traditional rulers within the centralized Islamic administrative framework of the
qs.e: Nupe emirates operated under Islamic administrative governance headed by Etsus.

qs.q: The 'Kofa' in the Hausa-Fulani Emirate system functioned as an essential intermediary or liaison officer between the district heads (Hakimi) and the
o: central Emir's court at the capital
qs.e: Kofas resided at the royal court, acting as diplomatic representatives and messengers for district Hakimis.

qs.q: The constitutional device of 'Igbe' in traditional Oyo political theory referred to the ritual obligation where an abusive or tyrannical Alaafin was forced to
o: surrender state territory to the Nupe Kingdom
abolish the Oyo Mesi council permanently
open the sacred calabash containing poison and end his life
qs.e: Receiving the empty calabash or parrot eggs signaled divine rejection, requiring the Alaafin to take poison.

qs.q: In Kanem-Borno constitutional history, the 'Mainin Kanendi' held the prestigious office of
o: Overseer of Royal Harem and Kitchens
Chief Justice and Chief Legal Advisor to the Mai
qs.e: Mainin Kanendi was the supreme legal authority and judicial advisor in the Mai's council.

qs.q: The 'Iyasere' in the pre-colonial Benin Kingdom served as the Prime Minister and head of the
qs.e: Chief Iyasere led the Town Chiefs, acting as premier chief and principal spokesman for the people.

qs.q: In traditional Ijaw city-state administration in the Niger Delta, governance was organized around the 'House System' (Oruwari), which served as a combined
o: military, commercial, and political trading corporation
qs.e: House Systems (Canoe Houses) were competitive commercial and defensive corporations led by prominent merchant chiefs.

qs.q: The primary reason why the British colonial administration adopted indirect rule in Northern Nigeria was the
o: existence of a well-organized traditional administrative system
complete absence of traditional rulers and local chiefs
presence of educated elite demanding direct governance
desire to establish a unitarian democratic political system
qs.e: Indirect rule succeeded in Northern Nigeria because the Fulani emirates possessed centralized administrative and judicial structures.

qs.q: Under the British colonial policy of indirect rule, traditional rulers served as the primary link between the
o: colonial government and the local population
foreign diplomatic corps and European traders
parliamentary opposition and civil service unions
qs.e: Indirect rule utilized traditional rulers to enforce colonial laws, collect taxes, and maintain order among local subjects.

qs.q: The French policy of assimilation aimed to transform African colonial subjects into
o: French citizens with full political rights
qs.e: Assimilation was designed to absorb African subjects into French culture, language, and constitutional citizenship.

qs.q: Which official held the highest executive authority in a British Crown Colony in West Africa?
qs.e: The Governor was the head of administration in a Crown Colony, representing the British monarch.

qs.q: The British colonial official responsible for supervising administration at the division level was the
qs.e: District Officers (DOs) oversaw local native authorities, inspected courts, and supervised tax collection at the divisional level.

qs.q: Which major historical event demonstrated popular resistance against the imposition of warrant chiefs and taxation in Eastern Nigeria?
qs.e: The Aba Women's War of 1929 was a major uprising against Warrant Chiefs and rumors of direct taxation on women.

qs.q: The system of Warrant Chiefs was introduced by the British colonial administration primarily in
qs.e: Because Eastern Nigeria lacked centralized monarchies, the British created artificial Warrant Chiefs to implement indirect rule.

qs.q: Indirect rule proved largely unsuccessful in Eastern Nigeria primarily because the traditional political system was
o: decentralized and segmentary without a single paramount authority
highly centralized under absolute constitutional monarchs
dominated by a powerful Islamic legal administrative framework
governed directly by an elected legislative council
qs.e: Igbo society operated a decentralized, village-based democratic system, making autocratic Warrant Chiefs incompatible.

qs.q: A major feature of the French colonial policy of association was the recognition of
o: indigenous African culture and institutions alongside French rule
total equality of all subjects with citizens of Paris
immediate independence for all overseas territories
exclusive reliance on British administrative doctrine
qs.e: Association replaced strict assimilation, allowing Africans to retain native customs under French colonial oversight.

qs.q: Native Authorities under British indirect rule were responsible for local administration, revenue collection, and the
o: command of national naval defense fleets
qs.e: Native Authorities collected taxes, maintained local police, and enforced customary laws under British supervision.

qs.q: The Indigénat code in French colonial West Africa gave colonial administrators summary power to
o: arrest and punish African subjects without trial
grant immediate university scholarships in Paris
elect representatives to the French National Assembly
appoint traditional emirs as sovereign kings
qs.e: The repressive Indigénat legal code allowed French officials to impose arbitrary fines and detention on non-citizen subjects.

qs.q: The introduction of direct taxation by colonial authorities in Western Nigeria led to widespread civil unrest, notably the
o: Abeokuta anti-tax protests led by market women
qs.e: Direct taxation imposed through sole native authorities provoked resistance, including the Abeokuta women's revolt.

qs.q: Which French West African communes enjoyed special status where residents automatically gained French citizenship rights?
o: Coastal regions of Dahomey and Togo
qs.e: Citizens of the Four Communes (Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque, Dakar) held French citizenship rights unlike general colonial subjects.

qs.q: The Native Treasury established under the British indirect rule system was designed to collect local taxes and fund
o: local public works and community administrative services
subsidies for British commercial shipping lines
campaign funds for Westminster parliamentary elections
qs.e: Native Treasuries retained a portion of tax revenue to finance local roads, native courts, and administrative salaries.

qs.q: Colonial legislative councils in British West Africa during the early twentieth century were dominated by
o: democratically elected indigenous trade union leaders
official British members and appointed representatives
sovereign emirs and paramount chiefs exclusively
qs.e: Early legislative councils had official majorities composed of British colonial officers, restricting native influence.

qs.q: Which factor significantly contributed to the breakdown of the policy of assimilation in French West Africa?
o: Widespread demand by French citizens for complete African independence
Resistance of Africans to abandoning their cultural identity and religion
Lack of financial resources in the French national treasury
Total refusal of colonial Africans to pay poll taxes
qs.e: Assimilation failed because Africans resisted surrendering their native customs, languages, and Islamic/traditional values.

qs.q: In Western Nigeria, indirect rule met with partial success because the traditional Obas were historically
o: absolute autocrats who ruled without any institutional restraint
subject to constitutional checks and balances by council of chiefs
purely religious figures with no political authority
appointed directly by European trading companies
qs.e: Yoruba Obas were checked by bodies like Oyomesi; indirect rule elevated their power autocratically, causing friction.

qs.q: The policy of indirect rule preserved traditional political institutions primarily to serve as
o: independent sovereign governments free from foreign control
inexpensive administrative instruments for colonial exploitation
democratic training grounds for immediate national self-rule
centers for scientific research and technological advancement
qs.e: Indirect rule minimized administrative costs for Britain by leveraging existing traditional hierarchies.

qs.q: Under British colonial rule, native courts were established to adjudicate cases primarily based on
o: customary laws and native traditions consistent with natural justice
qs.e: Native courts handled civil and minor criminal matters using local customary law, subject to colonial review.

qs.q: The dual mandate theory advocated by Lord Lugard held that European powers had a responsibility to develop Africa for
o: the exclusive enrichment of European imperial treasuries
the mutual benefit of both the industrial nations and the indigenous inhabitants
the immediate establishment of sovereign democratic republics
the total conversion of native populations to Western religion
qs.e: Lugard argued that colonization should benefit European trade while advancing African material welfare.

qs.q: Which administrative structure in British West Africa was responsible for advising the Governor on policy implementation?
qs.e: The Executive Council comprised senior colonial officials who advised the Governor on executive administration.

qs.q: The appointment of Warrant Chiefs in non-centralized societies of Eastern Nigeria alienated the populace because Warrant Chiefs
o: refused to collect taxes for the colonial government
lacked traditional legitimacy and abused their administrative powers
were elected exclusively by radical educated elites
abolished all native customary laws and traditional courts
qs.e: Warrant Chiefs were viewed as illegitimate colonial puppets who acted corruptly without traditional checks.

qs.q: Comparing British indirect rule with French assimilation, a major structural difference was that indirect rule
o: granted full citizenship to all subjects immediately
preserved native customs, whereas assimilation sought to replace indigenous culture with European culture
abolished all traditional chieftaincy institutions completely
operated without any European administrative supervisors
qs.e: Indirect rule operated through native institutions, while assimilation aimed to replace native culture with French culture.

qs.q: The British policy of indirect rule was criticized by educated African elites primarily because it
o: granted excessive political power to trade union organizations
excluded educated professionals from local governance in favor of traditional chiefs
forced all educated Africans to relocate to rural provinces
banned private legal practice in colonial courts
qs.e: Educated elites were marginalized from administration while uneducated traditional rulers were favored by colonial officers.

qs.q: Under the French colonial regime, the category of Africans designated as 'sujets' were subject to
o: full voting rights in the French Parliament
forced labor, compulsory military service, and arbitrary legal punishment
automatic appointment to colonial executive councils
qs.e: Non-citizen 'sujets' lacked constitutional rights and were subjected to forced labor (corvée) and the Indigénat.

qs.q: The Chief Secretary to the Government in a British West African colony functioned as the
o: chief justice of the colonial supreme court
presiding officer of the regional native court of appeal
head of the civil service and principal administrative assistant to the Governor
qs.e: The Chief Secretary coordinated government departments and acted as the chief administrative officer below the Governor.

qs.q: Which revenue source constituted the main financial foundation of the Native Treasuries under indirect rule?
o: Import tariffs on foreign industrial manufactured goods
Grants-in-aid from the League of Nations
Direct community tax and cattle tax (Jangali)
Corporate income tax on European mining syndicates
qs.e: Direct personal taxes and cattle tax (Jangali) funded Native Treasuries in colonial provinces.

qs.q: The West African Students' Union (WASU), formed in London, played a significant role in colonial politics by
o: supporting the permanent retention of British indirect rule
advocating the introduction of French assimilation policy
mobilizing anti-colonial sentiment and demanding constitutional reforms
suppressing trade union strikes across West Africa
qs.e: WASU served as a focal point for anti-colonial agitation and nurtured future West African nationalist leaders.

qs.q: In British West Africa, Crown Colonies differed from Protectorates because Crown Colonies were
o: independent sovereign nations under British protection
administered directly by traditional emirs without European control
annexed British territories where inhabitants were British subjects
governed exclusively by military martial law
qs.e: Crown Colonies (like Lagos) were formal British territories, whereas Protectorates were governed under treaty arrangements.

qs.q: The policy of direct rule in European colonialism is characterized by
o: exclusive reliance on traditional chiefs to manage local affairs
granting immediate self-determination to native populations
the complete displacement of indigenous rulers by European administrative personnel
qs.e: Direct rule bypasses traditional rulers, placing European officials in direct control of administration.

qs.q: The National Congress of British West Africa (NCBWA) advocated key reforms in the early 1920s, including the
o: immediate military invasion of French West African territories
total abolition of all Western education in West Africa
introduction of the elective principle and establishment of a West African university
creation of a single monarchical empire across West Africa
qs.e: NCBWA demanded elective representation, judicial reforms, and higher education opportunities for West Africans.

qs.q: Which factor prompted Britain to extend its administrative control over the hinterlands of Nigeria in the late nineteenth century?
o: Request by indigenous emirs for British military protection
Decision by the League of Nations allocating territory
Desire to secure trade monopolies and prevent rival European colonial expansion
Popular vote organized among traditional village councils
qs.e: Economic interests and inter-European scramble for Africa drove territorial annexation.

qs.q: Under the French policy of assimilation, an African subject could attain citizenship status (Évolué) primarily through
o: accumulating vast herds of livestock in rural areas
serving as a traditional chief in a local village
literacy in French, Western education, and abandonment of native customary practices
paying higher customs duties on agricultural exports
qs.e: Citizenship required adoption of French language, culture, Christian/secular lifestyle, and educational qualifications.

qs.q: The resistance of the Aba women against colonial authorities was triggered by rumors that
o: traditional chiefs were to be replaced by French colonial officers
all local markets were to be privatized by European companies
women were about to be subjected to direct taxation by native administration
female education was to be made compulsory in all schools
qs.e: Re-assessment of head counts created fears that women would be taxed alongside men, triggering widespread riots.

qs.q: The structural conflict within British indirect rule arose because traditional rulers were accountable to
o: their local electorate through periodic secret ballot voting
the International Court of Justice in Hague
the British colonial authorities rather than to their own indigenous subjects
the elected members of the regional legislative house
qs.e: Indirect rule turned chiefs into administrative agents of colonial authority, severing traditional accountability.

qs.q: Which colonial administrative council exercised both legislative and executive functions prior to constitutional separation of powers?
qs.e: Early Executive Councils frequently drafted regulations and exercised executive control simultaneously.

qs.q: The French policy of assimilation proved unworkable in West Africa largely because it
o: granted absolute sovereignty to indigenous African monarchs
required European settlers to adopt African traditional religions
assumed French culture was superior and ignored deeply rooted African traditions
banned all French commercial enterprises from trading in West Africa
qs.e: Ethnocentric assumptions underlying assimilation clashed with established West African social and religious structures.

qs.q: In Northern Nigeria, the British modified the traditional Islamic judicial system by subjecting Emir's court decisions to
o: total replacement with French civil code courts
immediate appeal to local village council elders
unilateral veto by elected trade union leaders
review and oversight by British administrative officers
qs.e: British officers supervised Native Courts, modifying punishments deemed contrary to British standards of natural justice.

qs.q: The Royal Niger Company's charter was revoked by the British Crown at the turn of the twentieth century, leading directly to the
o: immediate declaration of Nigerian national independence
creation of the Economic Community of West African States
expulsion of all European merchants from West Africa
establishment of formal British protectorates over Nigeria
qs.e: Revocation of the company charter marked the transition from corporate trading rule to formal British imperial governance.

qs.q: Colonial economic policies in West Africa were primarily structured to promote the
o: rapid industrial manufacturing of heavy capital goods locally
equal distribution of wealth among all indigenous peasants
total prohibition of foreign commercial imports
export of raw agricultural and mineral materials to European industries
qs.e: Colonial economies were structured extractively to supply raw materials (palm oil, groundnuts, cocoa, minerals) to Europe.

qs.q: The introduction of sole native authority status under indirect rule increased the power of traditional rulers by making them
o: directly elected by popular vote of rural citizens
subject to annual recall petitions by local assemblies
completely subordinate to regional legislative assemblies
independent of traditional council checks and balances
qs.e: Sole Native Authority designation vested power in individual chiefs, removing customary council checks.

qs.q: Which West African nationalist movement led by Casely Hayford sought political reforms across British West African territories?
o: National Congress of British West Africa
qs.e: NCBWA brought together leaders from Nigeria, Gold Coast, Sierra Leone, and Gambia to push for constitutional reform.

qs.q: The System of Association in French colonial administration differed from Assimilation by
o: granting immediate independence to all overseas colonies
forcing all West Africans to speak French exclusively at home
abolishing all European administrative presence in West Africa
respecting native institutions while maintaining French political dominance
qs.e: Association recognized indigenous institutions as subordinate instruments under French supervision.

qs.q: Which factor accounted for the strong opposition of educated elites to the Native Authority system?
o: Its insistence on democratic elections for all village posts
Its high expenditure on free university education
Its total prohibition of European trade monopolies
The system autocratic nature and exclusion of Western-educated Africans
qs.e: Educated elites viewed the Native Authority system as autocratic, reactionary, and an obstacle to modern governance.

qs.q: During the colonial period, the West African Currency Board (WACB) was established primarily to
o: provide interest-free loans to peasant farmers
subsidize industrial manufacturing factories in Lagos
issue and manage a stable unified currency pegged to the British pound
qs.e: WACB managed currency issuance across British West Africa, maintaining parity with sterling.

qs.q: The fundamental contradiction of the British indirect rule policy in West Africa was that it attempted to build a modern state using
o: communist economic planning frameworks alien to traditional African traders
direct parliamentary elections imported directly from European capital cities
purely military martial law courts lacking civil judicial procedures
feudal and traditional institutions incapable of accommodating modern political developments
qs.e: Indirect rule relied on traditional chieftaincy, which could not absorb modern democratic and nationalistic demands.

qs.q: In the French colonial empire, the decree system of legislation meant that laws were enacted primarily through
o: debates and votes in elected territorial assemblies across West Africa
referendums conducted among traditional village elders
judgments delivered by traditional religious courts
executive decrees issued directly by the French Ministry of Colonies or Governor-General
qs.e: Colonial legislation in French Africa was enacted via executive decrees rather than representative parliamentary debate.

qs.q: The failure of indirect rule in Eastern Nigeria highlighted the administrative error of
o: granting excessive democratic freedom to local village assemblies
abolishing all colonial revenue collection and taxation
appointing British governors who spoke local dialects fluently
imposing centralized autocratic institutions on segmentary, egalitarian societies
qs.e: Applying Northern-style centralized administration to decentralized Igbo political structures caused institutional failure.

qs.q: Which mechanism allowed British colonial governors to pass legislation despite opposition from unofficial members of the Legislative Council?
o: Unanimous consent requirements of traditional emirs
Mandatory approval by the International Court of Justice
Referendum votes cast by civil service employees
Governor's reserve powers of veto and certification
qs.e: The Governor could override Legislative Council decisions and enact bills using reserve powers.

qs.q: The Lugardian administrative model of indirect rule operated on the core doctrine of
o: complete assimilation of indigenous populations into British culture
total military occupation without native administrative involvement
immediate transition to multi-party democratic government
governance through existing native authorities under ultimate British sovereignty
qs.e: Indirect rule sought to govern through existing native authorities supervised by British personnel.

qs.q: The elective principle was first introduced into Nigerian colonial politics by the
qs.e: The Clifford Constitution introduced elective representation for Lagos and Calabar legislative seats.
