qs.q: Setting an initially high price for a new innovative product to recover development costs quickly before competitors enter (scenario #31) is
qs.e: Market skimming sets high initial prices to skim maximum revenues layer-by-layer from eager segments.

qs.q: Price skimming as a new product pricing strategy involves setting an initial price that is
o: below variable unit production costs to gain volume
identical to the industry benchmark going rate
high to skim maximum revenue step-by-step from willing market segments before competitors enter
determined solely by government price control boards
qs.e: Price skimming sets a high initial price to generate maximum profit from early adopters before lowering it later.

qs.q: Penetration pricing strategy aims to capture substantial market share rapidly by setting an initial price that is
o: extremely high to signal prestige status
equal to double unit fixed overhead costs
variable based on daily customer negotiation
low to attract a large volume of price-sensitive buyers quickly
qs.e: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to gain deep market penetration and high sales volume rapidly.

qs.q: Which internal factor heavily influences a manufacturing firm's pricing decisions?
o: Production costs and overall corporate marketing objectives
qs.e: Unit production costs and organizational marketing objectives are primary internal determinants of pricing floors.

qs.q: A retail price tag ending in .99 (such as ₦4,999 instead of ₦5,000) is a classic application of
qs.e: Odd-even psychological pricing uses prices ending in odd digits (.99) to make products feel significantly cheaper.

qs.q: A price reduction offered to buyers who pay their invoices promptly within ten days is known as a
qs.e: Cash discounts (e.g. 2/10 net 30) reward buyers for early cash payment, improving the seller's cash flow.

qs.q: Which pricing method adds a standard markup percentage to the total unit cost of producing a product?
qs.e: Cost-plus pricing calculates total unit cost and adds a fixed percentage margin to establish the final selling price.

qs.q: When demand for a product changes significantly in response to a minor shift in price, the demand is classified as
qs.e: Price elastic demand means consumers are highly price-sensitive, so small price changes produce large volume changes.

qs.q: Captive product pricing is exemplified when a manufacturer prices a main product (e.g. razor handle) low and its complementary consumable (e.g. razor blades)
o: at a high price margin because consumers are locked into purchasing it
strictly according to government price ceilings
qs.e: Captive pricing sells the core unit cheaply while making high profit margins on required ongoing accessories/supplies.

qs.q: Product bundle pricing involves selling several complementary items together in a combined package at a price that is
o: higher than purchasing each item individually
lower than the sum of buying each item separately
qs.e: Product bundling offers a suite of products together at a discounted total price compared to standalone prices.

qs.q: A trade discount (functional discount) is granted by a manufacturer to channel intermediaries in exchange for
o: performing marketing functions like warehousing, selling, and record-keeping
qs.e: Trade discounts compensate wholesalers and retailers for performing essential distribution and promotional services.

qs.q: Target return pricing calculates selling price based on achieving a specified
o: percentage return on investment (ROI) at target sales volume
qs.e: Target return pricing sets price to earn a targeted rate of return on invested capital given an expected sales volume.

qs.q: In going-rate pricing, a firm bases its prices primarily on
o: its own historical marginal production costs
competitors' prices rather than its own costs or demand considerations
qs.e: Going-rate pricing mirrors prevailing industry price levels, commonly seen in oligopolistic or homogenous product markets.

qs.q: What happens to total revenue when a seller increases the price of a product with highly elastic demand?
o: Total revenue decreases because percentage drop in quantity demanded exceeds percentage price increase.
qs.e: When demand is elastic, price increases cause a disproportionately larger fall in volume, driving down total revenue.

qs.q: Deceptive pricing practices forbidden under consumer protection laws include 'bait-and-switch', where a seller
o: offers genuine volume discounts on bulk orders
grants cash discounts for prompt payment
advertises an unrealistically low price to attract buyers but refuses to sell that item and pushes a pricier alternative
qs.e: Bait-and-switch deceptively advertises bargain items to lure customers into stores, then pressure them into buying expensive items.

qs.q: Dynamic pricing (real-time pricing) refers to the practice of
o: setting fixed prices that never change for five years
continuously adjusting prices to match real-time shifts in demand, supply, customer profiles, and competitive conditions
relying on printed price catalogs exclusively
qs.e: Dynamic pricing uses algorithms to adjust prices fluidly based on real-time market demand and capacity (e.g. airline seats, ride-hailing).

qs.q: Geographical pricing where the manufacturer charges the same delivered price to all buyers regardless of their physical distance from the factory is called
qs.e: Uniform delivered pricing charges all customers the same freight fee regardless of location (equal delivered price).

qs.q: A manufacturer has fixed costs of ₦1,200,000 per month. The variable cost per unit is ₦300, and the selling price is set at ₦500 per unit. Calculate the break-even output volume in units.
qs.e: Contribution margin = ₦500 - ₦300 = ₦200 per unit. Break-even volume = Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin = ₦1,200,000 / ₦200 = 6,000 units.

qs.q: A product cost ₦800 to produce. If the retailer applies a 25% markup on the selling price, what is the final selling price to the consumer?

When the price of a household electronic item was reduced from ₦50,000 to ₦45,000 (a 10% price drop), monthly quantity demanded increased from 1,000 units to 1,200 units (a 20% quantity increase). What is the price elasticity of demand?
qs.e: Price elasticity of demand = (% change in Qty) / (% change in Price) = 20% / 10% = 2.0 (elastic).

qs.q: Consumer goods that buyers purchase frequently, immediately, and with minimal comparison effort (scenario #1) are classified as
qs.e: Convenience goods are purchased routinely, frequently, and with minimal comparison effort.

qs.q: Goods for which consumers compare quality, price, and style across several stores before buying (case #16) are
qs.e: Shopping goods involve consumer comparison of suitability, quality, price, and style across stores.

qs.q: The fundamental service or benefit that the consumer is truly buying when purchasing a product (scenario #31) is the
qs.e: The core benefit represents the fundamental problem-solving benefit the consumer buys.

qs.q: In marketing, a product is most comprehensively defined as
o: only physical tangible items sold in retail shops
anything that can be offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use, or consumption that satisfies a want or need
raw materials harvested directly from agricultural land
services provided by government agencies exclusively
qs.e: A product encompasses physical goods, services, events, experiences, persons, places, properties, organizations, information, and ideas.

qs.q: Goods that consumers purchase frequently, immediately, and with minimal comparison or shopping effort are classified as
qs.e: Convenience goods (e.g. soap, milk, newspapers) are bought frequently with minimal decision effort.

qs.q: The fundamental problem-solving benefit or core service that a consumer is truly buying when purchasing a product is known as the
qs.e: The core benefit represents the basic fundamental solution or need satisfied (e.g., buying 'transportation' when purchasing a car).

qs.q: Items like chewing gum, magazines, and chocolates bought at the checkout counter on the spur of the moment are examples of
qs.e: Impulse goods are purchased spontaneously without prior planning or search effort.

qs.q: Products that consumers do not know about or know about but do not normally think of buying (such as life insurance or burial plots) are
qs.e: Unsought goods require active promotional effort and personal selling because buyers do not spontaneously seek them out.

qs.q: Consumer goods for which buyers spend considerable time and effort comparing suitability, quality, price, and style across stores are called
qs.e: Shopping goods (e.g. clothing, furniture, major appliances) involve comparison shopping across competing brands before buying.

qs.q: Specialty goods are characterized by
o: widespread intensive distribution in every neighborhood kiosk
unique brand characteristics or high brand luxury status for which buyers are willing to make special purchasing effort
qs.e: Specialty goods (e.g. luxury wristwatches, designer attire) possess unique status where buyers insist on specific brands.

qs.q: In the three-level product model, additional customer services and benefits such as warranty, free delivery, installation, and repair service constitute the
qs.e: The augmented product builds around the core and actual product by adding extra supportive services and warranties.

qs.q: Product mix width refers to the
o: total physical length of warehouse storage shelves
number of color variants per single product
number of different product lines carried by a manufacturing firm
average shelf lifespan of perishable food items
qs.e: Product mix width counts the total number of distinct product lines offered by the company (e.g., beverages, personal care, home care).

qs.q: Product line depth refers to the
o: number of distinct product lines carried by the company
number of different versions or variants offered for each product within a line
total revenue generated by the line
geographic spread of retail outlets stocking the line
qs.e: Depth measures how many variants (sizes, flavors, formulations) exist within each product in a line.

qs.q: The first formal stage in the New Product Development (NPD) process where new ideas are systematically gathered is
qs.e: Idea generation is the systematic search for new product concepts from internal and external sources.

qs.q: Idea screening in the New Product Development process is performed primarily to
o: build high-speed factory automated production lines
spot good ideas and drop poor or unviable ideas as early as possible
qs.e: Screening filters out unfeasible or unprofitable concepts early, preventing unnecessary development expenditure.

qs.q: Industrial goods purchased by manufacturing companies that enter the buyer's product directly as physical components are classified as
qs.e: Materials and parts (raw materials and manufactured component parts) become physical elements of the finished manufactured product.

qs.q: A manufacturer of mid-range family automobiles introduces a new luxury electric vehicle line targeted at affluent buyers. This product line decision is an example of
qs.e: Upward line stretching enters the high end of the market to achieve higher margins, prestige, or growth.

qs.q: Product line filling involves adding more items within the existing range of a product line to
o: shift entirely to raw material extraction
reduce overall company product line width to zero
plug market gaps, utilize excess manufacturing capacity, and satisfy full-line customer expectations
qs.e: Line filling adds extra items within present boundaries to satisfy more buyer variations and hold off competitors.

qs.q: During the business analysis stage of New Product Development, management evaluates the project's
o: projected sales, cost estimates, and profit projections to determine if they satisfy company financial objectives
qs.e: Business analysis reviews sales, cost, and profit projections to evaluate financial viability before physical development.

qs.q: Capital items in industrial goods classification differ from operating supplies because capital items
o: are consumed completely within one day of purchase
consist of routine office paper and paperclips
are long-lasting goods (like factory buildings and heavy machinery) that facilitate developing or managing the finished product
are purchased strictly for immediate resale without modification
qs.e: Capital goods are long-term industrial assets (installations and equipment) used in manufacturing operations over years.

qs.q: When a firm introduces a physical prototype of a new product to test its engineering functionality and safety in laboratories, it is in the stage of
qs.e: Product development turns abstract concept ideas into a physical, functional prototype for rigorous testing.

qs.q: Product mix consistency evaluates how closely related the various product lines are in terms of their
o: end-use requirements, production specs, distribution channels, or target markets
qs.e: Consistency measures how closely aligned various product lines are in production, distribution, and target markets.

qs.q: Concept testing differs from test marketing because concept testing evaluates
o: full commercial sales in thirty retail stores
the symbolic statement or written representation of a product idea with target consumers before building a physical prototype
qs.e: Concept testing tests descriptions or visual sketches of product concepts with target consumers early in development.

qs.q: A company manufacturing premium household soap decides to remove three unprofitable fragrance variants from its product line. This action is known as product line
qs.e: Line pruning or rationalization drops unprofitable, slow-moving items from a line to optimize profitability.

qs.q: Product cannibalization occurs when a firm introduces a new product item that
o: is immediately copied by foreign manufacturers
doubles total market growth for all industry players
steals sales volume and market share directly from the firm's own existing products rather than competitors
qs.e: Cannibalization happens when a new brand item eats into the sales and profits of the firm's established items.

qs.q: Emergency convenience goods are purchased by consumers when
o: an urgent, unexpected need arises (e.g. umbrellas during a sudden rainstorm or tire repair kits during a blowout)
they go on summer vacation overseas
qs.e: Emergency goods are bought immediately when an urgent need arises, with price taking secondary priority.

qs.q: Which factor is a leading cause of new product failure in fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) markets?
o: Overestimating market size and failing to differentiate the product meaningfully from existing alternatives
qs.e: Poor differentiation, inadequate market research, and overestimating demand account for most new product failures.

qs.q: Heterogeneous shopping goods differ from homogeneous shopping goods because consumers view heterogeneous goods as
o: differing significantly in product features, design, and quality, making features more important than minor price differences
qs.e: Heterogeneous shopping goods (e.g. clothing, furniture) differ in style and features, making design more critical than price.

qs.q: Product differentiation strategies focus on creating real or perceived differences in products through attributes like
o: features, performance quality, durability, reliability, repairability, and aesthetic design
using plain unprinted outer shipping crates
qs.e: Differentiation distinguishes a product from competitors across physical design, performance, reliability, and styling.

qs.q: Commercialization, the final step in New Product Development, involves
o: full-scale mass production launch and introducing the product into the commercial marketplace
qs.e: Commercialization executes full-scale production rollout, distribution buildup, and launch advertising.

qs.q: A manufacturer of luxury commercial jet aircraft extends its product line downwards by launching low-cost turboprop commuter planes. This downward line stretching risks
o: damaging the company's elite luxury brand image and cannibalizing higher-margin lines
qs.e: Downward stretching risks diluting high-end prestige image and cannibalizing sales from premium models.

qs.q: Industrial supplies (operating supplies) are characterized as the industrial equivalent of consumer
o: convenience goods because they are bought with minimum effort on a routine basis
qs.e: Operating supplies (lubricants, paper, cleaning items) are routine, low-cost items purchased frequently with minimal effort.

qs.q: When a company manages its product portfolio using the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Matrix, products with high market share in a slow-growing industry are classified as
qs.e: Cash Cows generate strong positive cash flow with low required reinvestment in mature, low-growth markets.

qs.q: In the BCG Matrix, products operating in high-growth markets but possessing low relative market share are called
qs.e: Question Marks require heavy cash investment to build market share in rapidly growing industries.

qs.q: Product design encompasses both ergonomics and aesthetics. Ergonomics in product design primarily ensures that the product
o: is priced lower than generic alternatives
uses the brightest neon colors on store shelves
is comfortable, safe, and efficient for human physical use
qs.e: Ergonomics focuses on human engineering—designing products for optimal human physical interaction, comfort, and safety.

qs.q: Which product mix dimension total reflects the average number of items carried across all product lines combined?
qs.e: Product mix length is the total number of items across all product lines in the company's portfolio.

qs.q: A trade-off that product managers face when expanding product line depth is
o: increased manufacturing and inventory holding costs versus better coverage of niche buyer preferences
total loss of trademark legal protection
inability to distribute through retail channels
qs.e: Deeper lines satisfy diverse consumer tastes but elevate inventory complexity, production changeover costs, and stockkeeping expenses.

qs.q: Feature fatigue occurs when a manufacturer adds so many extra complex features to a product that consumers feel
o: delighted by the low purchase price
overwhelmed, frustrated, and unable to operate the product easily
compelled to buy ten units simultaneously
qs.e: Feature fatigue happens when feature overload complicates user operation and reduces overall satisfaction.

qs.q: Simulated test marketing (laboratory test marketing) is chosen over traditional field test marketing primarily because it
o: eliminates the need for physical prototypes
is faster, less expensive, and keeps the new product secret from competitors
qs.e: Simulated test marketing exposes target buyers to products in artificial store setups, saving time and keeping plans confidential.

qs.q: Product durability measures the expected
o: visual brightness of primary package ink
speed of delivery from factory to retail store
operational lifespan of a product under normal or stressful operating conditions
number of retail shelf restocks per week
qs.e: Durability quantifies the physical longevity or operational life of a product before physical breakdown.

qs.q: Product reliability indicates the probability that a product will
o: double in value over ten years
function without malfunction or failure within a specified time period
be re-sold at a higher secondhand price
be featured on national news broadcasts
qs.e: Reliability reflects consistent, defect-free performance over time without unexpected failure.

qs.q: Which industrial goods category includes heavy equipment like diesel generators, stamping presses, and factory conveyor systems?
qs.e: Installations represent major capital investments (buildings, heavy machinery) that directly shape production operations.

qs.q: Accessory equipment in industrial goods differs from major installations because accessory equipment
o: has a useful lifespan of over fifty years
is bought through high-level board of director approval exclusively
includes portable tools and office equipment that facilitate factory operations without becoming part of the main building or heavy machinery
qs.e: Accessory equipment (hand tools, lift trucks, desktop computers) supports operations but involves smaller capital outlay than installations.

qs.q: A consumer goods company carries 4 product lines: Personal Care (8 items), Food & Beverage (12 items), Home Cleaning (6 items), and Health Care (10 items). What is the product mix length of the company?
qs.e: Product mix length = total items across all lines = 8 + 12 + 6 + 10 = 36 items.

qs.q: A manufacturer evaluated 200 new product ideas during idea generation. Idea screening rejected 75% of them. How many new product concepts passed screening to advance to the concept development stage?
qs.e: Rejected = 75% of 200 = 150. Advanced concepts = 200 - 150 = 50 concepts (or 25% of 200 = 50).

qs.q: A company invested ₦10,000,000 in developing a new food product. Business analysis projects annual unit sales of 50,000 units with a contribution margin of ₦100 per unit. How many years of sales are required to pay back the initial development investment?
qs.e: Annual contribution = 50,000 * ₦100 = ₦5,000,000. Payback period = ₦10,000,000 / ₦5,000,000 = 2 years.

qs.q: A factory produces 10,000 units of a consumer appliance. Quality control testing identified 200 defective units. What is the product reliability success rate percentage?
qs.e: Defect rate = (200 / 10,000) * 100% = 2%. Reliability success rate = 100% - 2% = 98%.

qs.q: A firm's flagship brand generated ₦20,000,000 in sales. After introducing a line extension, the new item generated ₦5,000,000 in sales, but ₦2,000,000 of those sales came from existing flagship brand buyers switching over. What was the net incremental revenue gain from the new line extension?
qs.e: Net incremental gain = New item sales - Cannibalized sales = ₦5,000,000 - ₦2,000,000 = ₦3,000,000.

qs.q: A company manufactures a product with a total manufacturing cost of ₦1,500 per unit. If warranty repair claims average 4% of total production and cost ₦500 per claim, what is the expected average warranty cost per manufactured unit?
qs.e: Expected warranty cost per unit = 4% * ₦500 = 0.04 * ₦500 = ₦20 per unit.

qs.q: A company carries 5 product lines with an average of 6 variants per line. If the company adds 2 new product lines with 5 variants each, what is the new total number of items in the company's product portfolio?
qs.e: Initial items = 5 * 6 = 30. Added items = 2 * 5 = 10. New total portfolio length = 30 + 10 = 40 items.

qs.q: The stage of the product lifecycle characterized by slow sales growth, high promotional expenditure, and negative profits (case #1) is the
qs.e: The introduction stage features slow sales rollout, high initial expenses, and heavy promotional investment.

qs.q: Rapid market acceptance, expanding sales volume, and peak profit margins typically occur during which stage of the PLC (scenario #16)?
qs.e: The growth stage sees rapid market expansion, increasing sales volume, and peaking profitability.

qs.q: A prolonged period of slowing sales growth where market saturation is reached and intense price competition emerges (case #31) is the
qs.e: Maturity is marked by market saturation, intense competition, and defensive strategies to preserve market share.

qs.q: A promotional push strategy relies primarily on directing promotional activities toward (scenario #1)
o: channel intermediaries like wholesalers and retailers
qs.e: Push strategies promote heavily to trade channel intermediaries to induce them to stock and sell product lines.

qs.q: A promotional pull strategy spends heavily on advertising and consumer promotion to induce (case #16)
o: factory workers to increase production speed
raw material suppliers to reduce prices
final consumers to demand the product from retailers
qs.e: Pull strategies focus on final consumers to create demand that pulls products through distribution channels.

qs.q: Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) requires an enterprise to integrate its promotional tools to deliver a (scenario #31)
o: different brand message across every channel
clear, consistent, and compelling brand message
flat wholesale price list to competitors
qs.e: IMC coordinates all communication touchpoints to deliver a unified, seamless, compelling message.

qs.q: A primary advantage of public relations and publicity over paid advertising in scenario #1 is its higher level of
o: direct control over message wording and timing
qs.e: Publicity is perceived as an objective news editorial, offering higher credibility than paid ad messages.

qs.q: A written commercial communication sent to journalists to announce news about an enterprise (case #16) is a
qs.e: Press releases provide journalists with structured news items to secure earned media coverage.

qs.q: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives build positive public relations by demonstrating an enterprise's commitment to (scenario #31)
o: maximizing short-term dividend payouts to shareholders strictly
ethical conduct, environmental sustainability, and community welfare
